The window shows "Checking the toolchain and the checkout…", spinner running, button disabled, for as long as it is left open.

So the stall is something about the app's own process that a terminal does not reproduce, and the app had already been quit by the time anyone looked — there was no stuck process left to
What was fixed is everything that made it undiagnosable, plus one genuine hazard found while reading the runner.

A probe that can report its own failure.

— so the last line in the log is the step that stalled.

returns when the pipe reaches EOF, and a pipe reaches EOF when every write end is closed. Foundation closes the parent's copy after the spawn, so normally the child's exit is enough — but any grandchild that inherited the descriptor keeps it open after the child is reaped, and

has already fired by then. The await on the exit signal returns and the process is gone, yet the read never finishes: a hang with a completed process and no error, which is exactly the shape observed. Draining on one thread that stops at EOF, and bounding the wait for that thread, removes the shape whether or not it was this session's cause.

The rest is diagnosis, not repair. An out-of-process step that cannot time out has only two outcomes, success and forever; adding the third makes the failure land in the window where the user is already looking.
Every out-of-process step in the updater is bounded.

A probe gets a hard limit and a kill. A build legitimately takes minutes, so it gets an idle clock (killed after 10 minutes without output — a build blocked on another build's lock prints one line and then nothing), a generous wall-clock limit, and a Cancel button while it runs. Every kill signals the process group, so the cargo and swift a script
s die with it instead of holding the lock. Nothing may have only "success" and "forever" as outcomes.
Log a step before running it, not after.
The log is the only account of where an update is sitting.
A probe reports why it could not answer.
A protocol method returning a bare collection ("which tools are missing") cannot say "the probe itself failed", and an empty result then reads as success. Give it a result type with a failure case.
Pick one reader. The streaming handler plus a bounded EOF signal covers both needs.
Sample the process while it is stuck.
gives the stack that a measurement from a terminal cannot; quitting the app first throws that away. This one is still open for want of that sample.
